title: Rise of the Womens Tennis Association
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Women play professional tennis all over the world today. The main group that runs this sport is the Womens Tennis Association. They govern the tour and work to help female athletes. Their main office is in Florida, with other offices in London and Beijing.
pages.caption: Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs in 1973, the same year King founded WTA

evidence.fileTitle: File:Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs 1973.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs in 1973, the same year King founded WTA

pages.text: In the past, women faced big money problems in tennis. Male leaders ran most tournaments and gave most of the cash to men. Later, a big tournament had a huge pay gap between men and women. Nine brave players decided to fight for equal pay.
pages.caption: Television, streaming, and social media would help connect the sport of tennis with more people around the world.

imageProvenance.credit: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA

evidence.fileTitle: File:2017 Citi Open Tennis Julia Goerges (36260415631).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Television, streaming, and social media would help connect the sport of tennis with more people around the world.

pages.text: These nine players became known as the Original 9. They made their own tournament in Houston with help from a magazine publisher and a tobacco company. This successful event led to more matches sponsored by Virginia Slims and other big brands.
pages.caption: WTA 1000 in Guadalajara

evidence.articleCaption: WTA 1000 in Guadalajara

pages.text: In June 1973, tennis star Billie Jean King helped found the Womens Tennis Association at a meeting in London. She became the first president of the new organization. Two years later, the group signed its very first television broadcast contract with CBS.
pages.caption: As the sport has grown over the years, more sponsorships help to keep the sport viable.

imageProvenance.credit: Keith Allison from Owings Mills, USA

evidence.articleCaption: As the sport has grown over the years, more sponsorships help to keep the sport viable.

pages.text: Over time, the association grew very large and gained huge sponsorships. After a long campaign, all four major tennis tournaments finally offered equal prize money to both women and men. Today, thousands of players from nearly one hundred countries compete for millions.

B1-B2.headline: Rise of the Womens Tennis Association

pages.text: The Womens Tennis Association stands as the principal organizing body for professional women's tennis worldwide. Headquartered in St. Petersburg, Florida, with regional hubs in London and Beijing, the association governs the professional tour to create a better future for female athletes globally.
pages.caption: Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs in 1973, the same year King founded WTA

evidence.fileTitle: File:Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs 1973.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs in 1973, the same year King founded WTA

pages.text: During the late 1960s and early 1970s, female tennis players encountered severe financial inequality within a male-dominated sport. Promoters and tournament directors routinely allocated the vast majority of prize money to male competitors, leading to extreme pay disparities at major sporting events.
pages.caption: Television, streaming, and social media would help connect the sport of tennis with more people around the world.

imageProvenance.credit: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA

evidence.fileTitle: File:2017 Citi Open Tennis Julia Goerges (36260415631).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Television, streaming, and social media would help connect the sport of tennis with more people around the world.

pages.text: Refusing to accept unfair treatment, nine top female athletes staged a historic protest by boycotting a tournament with a twelve-to-one pay gap. Backed by supporters, they organized their own successful competition in Houston, laying the vital groundwork for a separate women's professional circuit.
pages.caption: WTA 1000 in Guadalajara

evidence.articleCaption: WTA 1000 in Guadalajara

pages.text: Led by Billie Jean King, seventy female players officially established the Womens Tennis Association in London just before the 1973 Wimbledon Championships. King assumed the role of first president, and shortly afterward, the organization secured its milestone television broadcast agreement with CBS.
pages.caption: As the sport has grown over the years, more sponsorships help to keep the sport viable.

imageProvenance.credit: Keith Allison from Owings Mills, USA

evidence.articleCaption: As the sport has grown over the years, more sponsorships help to keep the sport viable.

pages.text: As the decades progressed, leadership figures negotiated major corporate sponsorships and expanded global reach. Following a determined campaign for financial parity, all four major tennis tournaments eventually achieved equal prize money for women and men, transforming the professional landscape.

C1-C2.headline: Evolution and Impact of the WTA

pages.text: Operating as the principal governing body of professional women's tennis, the Womens Tennis Association administers the worldwide tour from its headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida, complemented by European and Asia-Pacific offices in London and Beijing respectively.

pages.text: In the nascent years of tennis's Open Era, female athletes navigated systemic financial marginalization within a male-dominated ecosystem. Because tournament directors and proprietors were predominantly former male players, revenue distribution heavily favored men, culminating in severe prize disparities.
pages.caption: Television, streaming, and social media would help connect the sport of tennis with more people around the world.

imageProvenance.credit: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA

pages.text: Catalyzed by an egregious pay disparity at the Pacific Southwest Championships, nine prominent female competitors initiated a watershed boycott. Spearheading an independent alternative in Houston, they established the commercial viability necessary for autonomous women's competition.
pages.caption: WTA 1000 in Guadalajara

evidence.articleCaption: WTA 1000 in Guadalajara

pages.text: Under the stewardship of Billie Jean King, the collective formalized into the Womens Tennis Association during a London assembly in June 1973. King inaugurated her tenure as founding president, and the organization swiftly augmented its financial standing through foundational media contracts.
pages.caption: As the sport has grown over the years, more sponsorships help to keep the sport viable.

imageProvenance.credit: Keith Allison from Owings Mills, USA

evidence.articleCaption: As the sport has grown over the years, more sponsorships help to keep the sport viable.

pages.text: Subsequent administrative leadership orchestrated lucrative multinational sponsorships and expanded global broadcasting agreements. Through sustained advocacy, the association ultimately secured historic prize money parity across all four major Grand Slam tournaments, cementing professional equality.

title: Ending Decades of Conflict in Colombia
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Colombia had a very long war. The government and the FARC rebel group wanted to stop fighting. They started peace talks in the city of Havana, Cuba to find a good way to end the conflict.
pages.caption: John Kerry speaks with Bernard Aronson before separate meetings with Colombian and FARC peace negotiators

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.fileTitle: File:Secretary Kerry Speaks With U.S. Special Envoy for the Colombian Peace Process Aronson Before Meetings With Colombian and FARC Peace Negotiators in Havana, Cuba (25850848732).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: John Kerry speaks with Bernard Aronson before separate meetings with Colombian and FARC peace negotiators

pages.text: In 2016, the leaders signed a final peace agreement. President Juan Manuel Santos and rebel commander Rodrigo Londoño made peace. But the people voted on the agreement in October 2016. Sadly, more voters said no than yes to the plan.
pages.caption: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signing the peace treaty with FARC leader Rodrigo Londono Echeverri

evidence.fileTitle: File:Jefa de Estado participa en ceremonia de la Firma de la Paz entre el Gobierno de Colombia y las FARC E.P. (29953487045).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signing the peace treaty with FARC leader Rodrigo Londono Echeverri

pages.text: The leaders did not give up. They made a new and changed agreement. On November 24, 2016, they signed this new plan. They sent it to Congress instead of holding another vote for the public to decide.
pages.caption: Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon addresses the crowd at the Colombian peace ceremony in Cartagena where Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord on September 26, 2016

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.articleCaption: Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon addresses the crowd at the Colombian peace ceremony in Cartagena where Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord on September 26, 2016

pages.text: Both houses of the Colombian Congress looked at the new agreement. They voted to approve it at the end of November. This official vote finally brought the long armed conflict to an end.
Many other countries and groups helped with the peace process. The United Nations also helped to watch and support the peace. Women joined the talks too, asking to be a big part of building peace.

B1-B2.headline: Ending Decades of Conflict in Colombia

pages.text: The Colombian peace process refers to formal negotiations between the government under President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC-EP guerrilla group. Their goal was to end a decades-long conflict. These historic talks began in September 2012 and were held mostly in Havana, Cuba.
pages.caption: John Kerry speaks with Bernard Aronson before separate meetings with Colombian and FARC peace negotiators

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.fileTitle: File:Secretary Kerry Speaks With U.S. Special Envoy for the Colombian Peace Process Aronson Before Meetings With Colombian and FARC Peace Negotiators in Havana, Cuba (25850848732).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: John Kerry speaks with Bernard Aronson before separate meetings with Colombian and FARC peace negotiators

pages.text: In 2016, leaders announced a final agreement. President Santos and FARC commander Rodrigo Londoño signed the first accord. However, when the agreement was put to a national referendum on October 2, 2016, it was narrowly rejected by voters, with 50.2% voting against the deal.
pages.caption: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signing the peace treaty with FARC leader Rodrigo Londono Echeverri

evidence.fileTitle: File:Jefa de Estado participa en ceremonia de la Firma de la Paz entre el Gobierno de Colombia y las FARC E.P. (29953487045).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signing the peace treaty with FARC leader Rodrigo Londono Echeverri

pages.text: Following the surprising defeat at the ballot box, negotiators quickly drafted a revised peace agreement. This new version was signed on November 24, 2016. Instead of organizing another public referendum, the government submitted the text directly to the Congress of Colombia for ratification.
pages.caption: Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon addresses the crowd at the Colombian peace ceremony in Cartagena where Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord on September 26, 2016

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.fileTitle: File:Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon Addresses the Crowd (29330649203).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon addresses the crowd at the Colombian peace ceremony in Cartagena where Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord on September 26, 2016

pages.text: Both houses of Congress reviewed and approved the new agreement on November 29 and 30, 2016. This legislative approval officially brought the long-running conflict to an end. The process had also involved secret exploratory meetings that started back in the spring of 2011.

Throughout the negotiations, the international community played a major role as a facilitator and guarantor. The United Nations Security Council even adopted unanimous resolutions to support the peace talks and help monitor compliance, ensuring strong global backing for the Colombian peace efforts.

C1-C2.headline: The Architecture of the Colombian Peace Accord

pages.text: The Colombian peace process encompasses the protracted negotiations executed between the administration of President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC-EP insurgency. Commencing formally in September 2012 primarily within Havana, Cuba, these diplomatic efforts sought to terminate an internal armed conflict.
pages.caption: John Kerry speaks with Bernard Aronson before separate meetings with Colombian and FARC peace negotiators

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.fileTitle: File:Secretary Kerry Speaks With U.S. Special Envoy for the Colombian Peace Process Aronson Before Meetings With Colombian and FARC Peace Negotiators in Havana, Cuba (25850848732).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: John Kerry speaks with Bernard Aronson before separate meetings with Colombian and FARC peace negotiators

pages.text: Subsequent to years of dialogue, leadership announced a final accord in 2016, signed by President Santos and insurgent commander Rodrigo Londoño Echeverri. Nevertheless, this initial iteration suffered a narrow defeat during the national plebiscite on October 2, 2016, wherein 50.2% of participating voters rejected the proposed terms.
pages.caption: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signing the peace treaty with FARC leader Rodrigo Londono Echeverri

evidence.fileTitle: File:Jefa de Estado participa en ceremonia de la Firma de la Paz entre el Gobierno de Colombia y las FARC E.P. (29953487045).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos signing the peace treaty with FARC leader Rodrigo Londono Echeverri

pages.text: Demonstrating institutional resilience, the negotiating parties formulated a revised peace agreement, which was duly signed on November 24, 2016. Eschewing a secondary public referendum, the executive branch elected to submit the revised text to the bicameral Congress of Colombia for legislative ratification.
pages.caption: Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon addresses the crowd at the Colombian peace ceremony in Cartagena where Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord on September 26, 2016

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.fileTitle: File:Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon Addresses the Crowd (29330649203).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon addresses the crowd at the Colombian peace ceremony in Cartagena where Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC leader Timoleón Jiménez signed a peace accord on September 26, 2016

pages.text: Both houses of Congress ratified the new agreement on November 29 and 30, officially ending the conflict. This followed a trajectory that included exploratory meetings in 2011, transitional justice frameworks, and mine clearance initiatives.

Notably, the peace architecture distinguished itself through extensive international mediation and institutional guarantees. The United Nations Security Council lent unprecedented unanimous backing via resolutions like S/RES/2261, establishing an external verification mechanism to monitor compliance with the finalized terms.

title: Uncovering the Majapahit Capital at Trowulan
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Trowulan is an old site in East Java. It covers about 100 square kilometres. Experts think this place was once the capital city of the Majapahit Empire. The empire took its name from the city, which was known as Majapahit or Wilwatikta long ago.
pages.caption: Sumur Upas excavation site, Trowulan, Mojokerto.

evidence.articleCaption: Sumur Upas excavation site, Trowulan, Mojokerto.

pages.text: Old texts tell us about the capital. A 14th-century poem and a Chinese source describe the royal palace. They talk about thick red brick walls, big gates, and clean buildings. The palace had rooms, courtyards, canals, and spaces for priests and nobles.
pages.caption: Candi Tikus bathing place

evidence.articleCaption: Candi Tikus bathing place

pages.text: Today, many relics are kept in the Trowulan Museum. Visitors can also see old ruins around the village. Some ruins are very damaged, but others have been fixed up. Most of these old buildings are made of red brick.
pages.caption: Brahu temple

evidence.articleCaption: Brahu temple

pages.text: People have found interesting sites around the area. One of them is Tikus Temple, which is a sunken bathing pool. Another is Wringin Lawang, a large split gate made of red brick. Experts think these structures date back to the Majapahit era.
pages.caption: Segaran pool

evidence.articleCaption: Segaran pool

pages.text: Archaeologists also found water canals, wells, and housing areas. These finds show that many people lived here long ago. In 2009, the government submitted Trowulan to the UNESCO World Heritage list to help protect the historic site.

B1-B2.headline: Uncovering the Majapahit Capital at Trowulan

pages.text: Trowulan is an archaeological site spanning roughly 100 square kilometres in East Java, Indonesia. Scholars have theorized that this expansive area served as the capital city of the powerful Majapahit Empire. The ancient city was known as Majapahit or Wilwatikta, giving the empire its name.
pages.caption: Sumur Upas excavation site, Trowulan, Mojokerto.

evidence.articleCaption: Sumur Upas excavation site, Trowulan, Mojokerto.

pages.text: Historical accounts provide a glimpse into the ancient capital. The 14th-century poem Nagarakretagama and a 15th-century Chinese source describe a walled royal compound featuring large gates, water canals, pavilions, and quarters for priests and nobles. However, because some poetic details are vague, researchers have reached different conclusions when trying to map the capital.
pages.caption: Candi Tikus bathing place

evidence.articleCaption: Candi Tikus bathing place

pages.text: While early research focused mainly on monumental tombs and temples, recent excavations have uncovered industrial areas, commercial zones, water supply systems, and dense habitation sites. Many artifacts from this period are housed in the Trowulan Museum, located near Segaran Pool.
pages.caption: Brahu temple

evidence.articleCaption: Brahu temple

pages.text: Several notable ruins survive across the landscape. Tikus Temple is a sunken ritual bathing pool featuring terraced structures. Wringin Lawang is a grand red brick split gate from the 14th century, which likely served a ceremonial purpose. Additionally, Brahu Temple stands as the sole surviving structure of a historic building cluster.
pages.caption: Segaran pool

evidence.articleCaption: Segaran pool

pages.text: Excavations have also revealed brick floors, wells, and drains, indicating an organized urban environment. Economic life was supported by markets using Chinese bronze coins, while clay piggy banks show how people saved money. To protect these historic remnants from damage, Indonesia submitted Trowulan to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2009.

Encompassing approximately 100 square kilometres in the East Java province of Indonesia, Trowulan is an archaeological site widely theorized to be the location of the eponymous capital of the Majapahit Empire. Historically referred to as Majapahit or Wilwatikta, the urban center was ultimately razed during an invasion by Girindrawardhana in 1478, prompting the relocation of the capital to Daha.
pages.caption: Sumur Upas excavation site, Trowulan, Mojokerto.

evidence.articleCaption: Sumur Upas excavation site, Trowulan, Mojokerto.

pages.text: Contemporary records, including Mpu Prapanca's 14th-century poem Nagarakretagama and a 15th-century Chinese account, furnish detailed descriptions of the royal compound and urban layout. These texts outline brick fortifications, gates, pavilions, and distinct quarters for nobility and clergy. Because certain poetic descriptions remain ambiguous, scholars compiling capital plans have arrived at divergent interpretations.
pages.caption: Candi Tikus bathing place

evidence.articleCaption: Candi Tikus bathing place

pages.text: Early investigations prioritized monumental religious architecture and tombs, but recent archaeological surveys have identified industrial, commercial, and residential sectors alongside sophisticated water supply networks. These findings collectively indicate a densely populated urban center during the 14th and 15th centuries, with many artifacts subsequently preserved in the Trowulan Museum.
pages.caption: Brahu temple

evidence.articleCaption: Brahu temple

pages.text: Prominent surviving structures include Tikus Temple, a sunken ritual bathing complex, and Wringin Lawang, a monumental 14th-century split gate constructed from red brick. Furthermore, Brahu Temple is believed to have functioned as a royal mortuary shrine, aligning with local traditions concerning the cremation sites of early Majapahit rulers.
pages.caption: Segaran pool

evidence.articleCaption: Segaran pool

pages.text: Subsurface excavations have revealed stratified residential remains equipped with wells and drainage systems. Economic activity relied heavily on imported Chinese bronze coins, which replaced previous currencies and facilitated specialized market transactions, as evidenced by the discovery of clay coin containers. In recognition of its immense historical value, Trowulan was submitted to the UNESCO World Heritage list in October 2009.

pages.text: Several notable ruins survive across the landscape. Tikus Temple is a sunken ritual bathing pool featuring terraced structures. Wringin Lawang is a grand red brick split gate from the 14th century, which likely served a ceremonial purpose. Additionally, Brahu Temple stands as the sole surviving structure of a historic building cluster.

pages.text: Excavations have also revealed brick floors, wells, and drains, indicating an organized urban environment. Economic life was supported by markets using Chinese bronze coins, while clay piggy banks show how people saved money. To protect these historic remnants from damage, Indonesia submitted Trowulan to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2009.

title: Building the India-Middle East-Europe Corridor

A1-A2.headline: A New Trade Route for India and Europe

pages.text: The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor is a new project. It wants to help trade grow between Asia and Europe. The path goes from India through the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Greece. It is based on a very old trade route.
pages.caption: Participating countries in the Belt and Road Initiative. Green = signed agreement with China. Light green = withdrawn. Yellow = de facto participant.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Countries of the Belt and Road Initiative.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Participating countries in the Belt and Road Initiative. Green = signed agreement with China. Light green = withdrawn. Yellow = de facto participant.

pages.text: In 2023, leaders met at the G20 Summit in New Delhi. India announced the project there. Many countries signed a paper about working together. These countries include India, the United States, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, Italy, and the European Union.
pages.caption: Future railway lines of Etihad Rail in the U.A.E. (2022)

evidence.articleCaption: Future railway lines of Etihad Rail in the U.A.E. (2022)

pages.text: The project uses different ways to move goods. The Eastern Corridor uses ships to go from India to the Persian Gulf. The Northern Corridor uses trains across countries like Saudi Arabia and Jordan, and then ships across the sea to Europe.
pages.caption: The destruction in Gaza in October 2023

imageProvenance.credit: WAFA (Q2915969) in contract with a local company (APAimages)‏‏

evidence.fileTitle: File:Damage in Gaza Strip during the October 2023 - 29.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The destruction in Gaza in October 2023

pages.text: The project also cares about clean energy and the environment. It wants to use green hydrogen and save fuel. This clean energy can help power trucks, trains, and ships. It gives Europe and other places a good choice for clean power.
pages.caption: President Tump and Prime Minister Modi at the White House in 2025

evidence.fileTitle: File:President Donald J. Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (03).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: President Tump and Prime Minister Modi at the White House in 2025

pages.text: Different countries have their own reasons to join. India wants to build trust and trade with others. The United Arab Emirates wants to be a big center for shipping. Germany wants to get clean energy imports from the Gulf region.

The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor is a planned infrastructure project designed to boost economic integration between Asia, the Persian Gulf, and Europe. The route connects India to Europe through the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Greece, drawing inspiration from ancient trade paths.
pages.caption: Participating countries in the Belt and Road Initiative. Green = signed agreement with China. Light green = withdrawn. Yellow = de facto participant.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Countries of the Belt and Road Initiative.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Participating countries in the Belt and Road Initiative. Green = signed agreement with China. Light green = withdrawn. Yellow = de facto participant.

pages.text: Diplomatic ties grew over many years through policies and new agreements like the Abraham Accords and the I2U2 group. The project was officially announced during the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi when leaders signed a Memorandum of Understanding.
pages.caption: Future railway lines of Etihad Rail in the U.A.E. (2022)

evidence.articleCaption: Future railway lines of Etihad Rail in the U.A.E. (2022)

pages.text: The transport network relies on a multimodal system. The Eastern Corridor uses maritime routes from India to the Persian Gulf. Meanwhile, the Northern Corridor uses an overland railway network across the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel, followed by shipping across the Mediterranean Sea to Europe.
pages.caption: The destruction in Gaza in October 2023

evidence.articleCaption: The destruction in Gaza in October 2023

pages.text: Sustainability is a major focus for the corridor. By using electric and multimodal routes, the project aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and save fuel compared to older shipping canals. It also plans to feature hydrogen pipelines and refueling hubs to supply clean energy for hard-to-abate sectors like steelmaking and transport.
pages.caption: President Tump and Prime Minister Modi at the White House in 2025

evidence.fileTitle: File:President Donald J. Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (03).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: President Tump and Prime Minister Modi at the White House in 2025

pages.text: Participating nations view the project through different strategic lenses. The United States aims to offer an alternative to China's Belt and Road Initiative and secure supply chains. India wants to serve as a trusted bridge of global connectivity, while European nations like Germany hope to diversify their energy imports.

Despite strong political backing, the agreement currently functions as a broad declaration of intent because it still lacks a detailed funding plan and concrete implementation mechanisms. Some regional leaders have also raised criticisms regarding its exclusion of certain nations and its reliance on specific transport methods.

C1-C2.headline: Strategic Realities of the IMEC Infrastructure Initiative

pages.text: The India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor represents a major transnational connectivity initiative intended to foster economic integration across Asia, the Persian Gulf, and Europe. Spanning an infrastructure route through the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Greece, the corridor seeks to revive historical trade patterns through modern multimodal logistics.
pages.caption: Participating countries in the Belt and Road Initiative. Green = signed agreement with China. Light green = withdrawn. Yellow = de facto participant.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Countries of the Belt and Road Initiative.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Participating countries in the Belt and Road Initiative. Green = signed agreement with China. Light green = withdrawn. Yellow = de facto participant.

pages.text: The institutional groundwork emerged from decades of geopolitical shifts, including India's Look West policy, the Abraham Accords, and the formation of the I2U2 grouping. These diplomatic precursors culminated in the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi, where representatives signed a foundational Memorandum of Understanding.
pages.caption: Future railway lines of Etihad Rail in the U.A.E. (2022)

evidence.articleCaption: Future railway lines of Etihad Rail in the U.A.E. (2022)

pages.text: Operationally, the infrastructure divides into an Eastern maritime corridor connecting Indian ports to the Persian Gulf and a Northern corridor utilizing overland rail networks across the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel. This combination of maritime, road, and rail transport is designed to enhance supply chain resilience against unexpected disruptions.
pages.caption: The destruction in Gaza in October 2023

imageProvenance.credit: WAFA (Q2915969) in contract with a local company (APAimages)‏‏

evidence.fileTitle: File:Damage in Gaza Strip during the October 2023 - 29.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The destruction in Gaza in October 2023

pages.text: Beyond physical transport, the project integrates environmental sustainability and digital innovation. It incorporates renewable energy frameworks, specifically green hydrogen pipelines and refueling hubs intended to decarbonize heavy sectors and lower fuel consumption relative to traditional canal transit. Furthermore, artificial intelligence and blockchain technologies are slated to optimize border customs and transit efficiency.
pages.caption: President Tump and Prime Minister Modi at the White House in 2025

evidence.fileTitle: File:President Donald J. Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi (03).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: President Tump and Prime Minister Modi at the White House in 2025

pages.text: Strategic motivations vary among participating states. For the United States, the corridor serves as a geopolitical counterweight to China's Belt and Road Initiative and secures critical supply chains via the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment. European participants view the project as an opportunity to diversify energy imports and align with regional decarbonization targets.

Notwithstanding its ambitious geopolitical scope, the initiative remains in a declaratory phase, currently lacking a comprehensive funding structure and definitive implementation schedules. External actors have also voiced criticisms regarding route exclusions and structural dependencies, highlighting the complex diplomatic landscape surrounding the corridor's prospective realization.

title: Understanding Open Access Publishing
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Open access lets people read published research without paying money or hitting walls. It helps share science and ideas with everyone around the world. The main focus is on research papers from academic journals.
pages.caption: Open access logo, originally designed by Public Library of Science

imageProvenance.credit: art designer at PLoS, modified by Wikipedia users Nina, Beao, and JakobVoss

evidence.articleCaption: Open access logo, originally designed by Public Library of Science

pages.text: Traditional journals charge fees for subscriptions. Open access journals use different ways to pay for publishing costs. They might rely on author fees or public money, subsidies, and sponsorships to stay open.
pages.caption: Download rate for articles on Sci-Hub (black open access)

evidence.articleCaption: Download rate for articles on Sci-Hub (black open access)

pages.text: People use different colors to name different types of open access. The most common names are green, gold, and hybrid. Each color shows a different way to share research with the public.
pages.caption: Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ

evidence.articleCaption: Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ

pages.text: In the gold model, publishers make articles free right away on their websites. Authors can also use green open access by posting their work on their own websites or in special digital repositories.
pages.caption: Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ

evidence.articleCaption: Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ

pages.text: Hybrid journals mix open access with closed access. They charge subscription fees, but authors can pay extra to make their specific articles free. Some journals also use other models to share research safely.

Open access is a set of principles and practices that delivers publications to readers free of access charges or other barriers. While strict open access also reduces barriers to copying and reuse, the primary focus of the movement has always been peer-reviewed academic journal literature.
pages.caption: Open access logo, originally designed by Public Library of Science

imageProvenance.credit: art designer at PLoS, modified by Wikipedia users Nina, Beao, and JakobVoss

evidence.articleCaption: Open access logo, originally designed by Public Library of Science

pages.text: Unlike traditional journals that rely on subscriptions or pay-per-view charges, open-access journals use funding models that do not require readers to pay. Instead, they often rely on author fees, public funding, subsidies, and sponsorships to cover costs across many formats like articles and reports.
pages.caption: Download rate for articles on Sci-Hub (black open access)

evidence.articleCaption: Download rate for articles on Sci-Hub (black open access)

pages.text: Different open access types are commonly described using a color system. The most widely recognized names are green, gold, and hybrid open access, though several alternative models are also used across the scholarly publishing landscape.
pages.caption: Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ

evidence.articleCaption: Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ

pages.text: In the gold model, publishers make all content available for free immediately with Creative Commons licenses for reuse. Green open access involves self-archiving, where authors post their work on independent repositories or institutional websites so people can download it for free.
pages.caption: Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ

evidence.articleCaption: Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ

pages.text: Hybrid journals contain a mixture of open and closed access articles. They are partially funded by subscriptions, providing free access only for individual articles where authors pay an extra publication fee. This specific model can be more expensive and sometimes controversial.

Other variations include bronze articles, which are free to read without clear reuse licenses, and diamond journals that charge no fees to readers or authors. Publishing models continue to evolve as institutions and researchers navigate the complex transition toward open science.

C1-C2.headline: The Structure and Evolution of Open Access

pages.text: Open access encompasses principles and practices designed to deliver nominally copyrightable publications without access charges or traditional barriers. Strict or libre open access further reduces reuse restrictions through open copyright licenses, focusing predominantly on peer-reviewed academic research literature.
pages.caption: Open access logo, originally designed by Public Library of Science

imageProvenance.credit: art designer at PLoS, modified by Wikipedia users Nina, Beao, and JakobVoss

evidence.articleCaption: Open access logo, originally designed by Public Library of Science

pages.text: Conventional journals sustain operations through access tolls such as subscriptions and pay-per-view charges. Conversely, open-access publications utilize alternative financial frameworks relying on author fees, public funding, and institutional subsidies, extending across diverse outputs including monographs, conference papers, and reports.
pages.caption: Download rate for articles on Sci-Hub (black open access)

evidence.articleCaption: Download rate for articles on Sci-Hub (black open access)

pages.text: The scholarly community commonly categorizes open access modalities through a descriptive color taxonomy. While green, gold, and hybrid represent the most prevalent designations, numerous alternative structures and specific naming conventions persist within the broader publishing ecosystem.
pages.caption: Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ

evidence.articleCaption: Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ

pages.text: Gold open access entails immediate dissemination via publisher websites under permissive sharing licenses. Alternatively, green open access facilitates author self-archiving, permitting researchers to deposit their manuscripts in institutional or independent central repositories to ensure barrier-free public access.
pages.caption: Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ

evidence.articleCaption: Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ

pages.text: Hybrid journals present a dual framework containing both open and closed articles, operating partially through subscriptions while levying additional publication fees for specific open content. Critics note that hybrid approaches frequently incur higher costs and can introduce controversial pricing dynamics.

Alternative models address different operational demands, such as diamond journals that eliminate fees for both readers and authors through external grants, or bronze articles that lack explicit reuse licenses. This ongoing structural transition continues to generate substantial debate among academic stakeholders globally.
